opus-5.5.text:
I don't think there's anything special about the human level from the point of view of the underlying technology. Human intelligence is where evolution happened to land, given a lot of constraints that just don't apply to machines: the size of the birth canal, the metabolic cost of a big brain, the speed of neurons, the fact that we can't copy ourselves or share what we've learned except slowly through language. None of those are fundamental limits on intelligence; they're limits on primates.

If you look at the narrower domains where we've already built systems, human level has never been a stopping point. In Go, chess, and protein structure prediction, systems went through human level and kept going, often quite quickly. Human performance was just one point on the curve.

There's a reasonable objection that current systems learn a lot from human data, so maybe imitation caps you near the level of the data. I take that seriously, but I don't think it holds up. Even pure imitation gives you something no human has: one system with the breadth of many experts at once, running faster, in many copies. And we're increasingly not relying on imitation alone. Reinforcement learning against verifiable outcomes, in maths and code for example, lets systems improve beyond their demonstrations, much as AlphaGo eventually stopped needing human games.

Then there's the feedback loop. Once systems are roughly as good as humans at AI research, you can run many of them in parallel, and they can help build the next generation. You don't need anything exotic like a sudden intelligence explosion for that to matter. Even a moderate speedup in research compounds.

So I'd put it the other way around: stalling right at human level would be the surprising outcome and would need a specific explanation. I don't know of a good one. That's a big part of why I work on safety. If capabilities do go past us, we need ways to oversee and trust systems that we can't directly check, and that's much easier to build before we need it than after.

r001.rationale: The response describes parallel AI systems helping with AI research, but does not say human supervision of short model runs enables progress beyond human-level intelligence.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a month of software-engineering work or the planning and subtle reasoning needed to complete it.

r003.rationale: It attributes continued progress to factors such as removing biological limits, reinforcement learning, and AI-research feedback loops, not to momentum from reaching the reasoning ability needed for long-horizon software-engineering tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that there's nothing special about the human level from the perspective of the underlying process that's producing capabilities. Human intelligence is the product of evolution operating under a bunch of constraints that have nothing to do with what's optimal: we have a skull of a certain size, a birth canal of a certain size, neurons that fire at maybe a couple hundred hertz, a brain that has to run on roughly twenty watts. None of those constraints apply to a system running in a datacenter. So if you ask "where should capabilities stop?", the human level is just a point we happen to be standing on. It's salient to us, but it's not a natural ceiling.

The second thing is the mechanism of progress. Right now, a lot of what's driving capabilities is scaling: more compute, more data, better algorithms, and these have been fairly predictable for a while. There's no particular reason those trends bend sharply at the point where the model is about as good as a person. If anything, you'd expect the opposite, because once systems are roughly human-level at the kind of work that produces AI progress, meaning ML research, writing code, running experiments, designing chips, they start contributing to their own improvement. That doesn't have to be some dramatic recursive explosion. Even a modest version, where AI systems make the researchers at labs substantially more productive, is already enough to keep the curve going past the point where we might have otherwise expected it to flatten.

There's also an argument from the structure of the systems themselves. Even a model that's "human-level" on average is not human-like in its profile. It can run many copies in parallel, it can be copied and modified, it can be trained directly on narrow skills rather than learning them over years, and it doesn't forget things or get tired. So "human-level" as a description is a bit misleading. A system that matches a human on some benchmark is already superhuman along several axes, and that suggests the plateau picture is just the wrong frame.

Now, I want to be honest that there are versions of the stall story I take seriously. Data could run out for certain kinds of tasks. Some capabilities might require feedback from the real world that's slow to get. There could be economic or regulatory constraints that slow deployment even if the underlying technology keeps improving. And there's some domain where human knowledge is the training signal, and it's not obvious how you exceed the ceiling of your teacher. But I don't think any of those produce a hard wall at exactly human level. They produce slowdowns, or unevenness across domains, which is quite different.

And the historical evidence we do have points the same way. In every narrow domain where we've gotten to human level, whether that's chess or Go or protein structure prediction, the systems didn't stop there. They kept going. It's reasonable to expect that generalizes, though obviously with more uncertainty about timelines than about the direction.

So my view is: if you're uncertain, the right prior is continued progress, and the question is more about the rate and the shape than about whether it happens. Which is a big part of why I think the safety work matters now rather than later. If you only start thinking about systems smarter than you once they exist, you've left it quite late.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think human-level intelligence is a particularly natural stopping point. It’s a level we happen to be very interested in because we’re humans, but it’s not obviously a fundamental limit on what computation can do.

Evolution produced our brains under a particular set of constraints: they have to fit in our heads, run on a small amount of energy, and develop within a human lifetime. Those aren’t the same constraints we face when building AI systems. We can give them more computation, and they can potentially learn from much more experience than any individual human.

There’s also a feedback loop once AI becomes good at research, including research on AI itself. That could help drive further progress. It doesn’t establish how fast that progress will be, or mean there won’t be bottlenecks. But for progress to stop at roughly human level, you’d need some reason that the methods which got us there suddenly cease to work at that particular point. I don’t see a strong reason to expect that.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t see a particular reason why human-level intelligence would be a stopping point. It’s a level that’s salient to us because we’re human, but it isn’t obviously a fundamental limit on what computation can do.

And “human-level” is already a slightly misleading picture. AI systems can be much better than us at some tasks while being worse at others. So I’d expect progress to look less like reaching a single threshold and more like getting better across a range of abilities.

Once systems are good enough to help with AI research, that also gives you a mechanism for further progress: they can help design algorithms, run experiments, and improve the next generation of systems. That doesn’t establish that you get an instantaneous intelligence explosion. There can still be bottlenecks involving compute, experiments, or the physical world. But it makes stalling precisely at the human level seem particularly unlikely.
